The third: *al-shahid* is the community of Muhammad ﷺ, because of His saying: ﴿لِّتَكُونُواْ شُهَدَآءَ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 143]. The fifth: *al-shahid* is all the prophets, and *al-mashhud* is their communities, because every prophet witnesses over his community; or the testimony is to their deeds; or the Day of Resurrection, because it is present in it.

The sixth: *al-shahid* is the guardian angels, and *al-mashhud* is people, because the angels witness over them; or the deeds, because the angels witness them; or the Day of Resurrection; or the Dawn Prayer, because of His saying: ﴿إِنَّ قُرْآنَ ٱلْفَجْرِ كَانَ مَشْهُوداً﴾ [Al-Isra: 78].

The seventh: *al-shahid* is all people, because they are present on the Day of Resurrection, i.e., they attend it, and *al-mashhud* is the Day of Resurrection, because of His saying: ﴿وَذَلِكَ يَوْمٌ مَّشْهُودٌ﴾ [Hud: 103].

﴿قُتِلَ أَصْحَابُ ٱلأُخْدُودِ﴾ The discussion here falls into three sections.

The first: concerning the answer to the oath, and there are four opinions on it. The first is that it is His saying: ﴿إِنَّ بَطْشَ رَبِّكَ لَشَدِيدٌ﴾ [Al-Buruj: 12]. The second is that it is: ﴿إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ فَتَنُواْ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَٱلْمُؤْمِنَاتِ﴾ [Al-Buruj: 10]. These two opinions are weak, because of the distance between the oath and the answer. The third is that it is "Qutila Ashab al-Ukhdud" (the companions of the trench were killed), with the implied meaning: "Surely they were killed." The fourth is that it is omitted, and is indicated by "Qutila Ashab al-Ukhdud," with the implied meaning: "Surely these disbelievers have been killed as the companions of the trench were killed." This is because the disbelievers of Quraysh used to torture those among their people who had embraced Islam, to make them turn back from Islam. So Allah mentioned the story of the companions of the trench as a warning to the disbelievers and as a consolation to the tortured Muslims.

The second section: explanation of its wording. As for *qutila*, it has been disputed whether it is a supplication or a statement; and whether it means killing literally or cursing. As for *al-ukhdud*, it is a cleft in the earth like a trench or the like. As for *ashab al-ukhdud*, it may mean the disbelievers who used to burn the believers in the trench, or it may mean the believers in the trench, or the believers who were burned in it. Then the killing would be a literal statement. The first is more apparent.

The third section: the story of the companions of the trench, which has four opinions. The first is what has come from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a long hadith, whose meaning is: a disbelieving king made the people of his city embrace (a false religion), so he ordered a trench to be dug, and it was dug at the mouths of the roads, and fires were kindled in it. The boy said to her: "O mother, be patient, for you are upon the truth."

The second: a king committed incest with his sister, then wanted to make marriage with sisters lawful for the people. Some people obeyed him, and among them the Magians took that (practice). Some people disobeyed him, so he dug a trench for them and burned them in it with fire.

The third opinion: the prophet of the companions of the trench was an Abyssinian, and the Abyssinians are the remnant of the companions of the trench.

The fourth opinion: the companions of the trench were Dhu Nuwas, who is mentioned in the story of 'Abdullah ibn al-Tamir which is widely known. It is possible that Dhu Nuwas is the king whom the Prophet ﷺ mentioned, so this opinion agrees with the first, for Dhu Nuwas dug a trench, kindled fires in it, and threw into it everyone who affirmed the Oneness of Allah Exalted and followed the righteous servant 'Abdullah ibn al-Tamir.

The third opinion: the prophet of the companions of the trench was an Abyssinian, and the Abyssinians are the remnant of the companions of the trench.

The fourth opinion: the companions of the trench were Dhu Nuwas, who is mentioned in the story of 'Abdullah ibn al-Tamir which is widely known. It is possible that Dhu Nuwas is the king whom the Prophet ﷺ mentioned, so this opinion agrees with the first, for Dhu Nuwas dug a trench, kindled fires in it, and threw into it everyone who affirmed the Oneness of Allah Exalted and followed the righteous servant 'Abdullah ibn al-Tamir.

﴿وَٱلسَّمَآءِ ذَاتِ ٱلْبُرُوجِ﴾ *Al-buruj* (the mansions, or constellations) are the well-known stations, and there are twelve of them, which the sun traverses in the year. It was also said that they are the great stars, because they *tabarraja*, meaning they appear (display themselves). ﴿وَٱلْيَوْمِ ٱلْمَوْعُودِ﴾ is the Day of Resurrection, by consensus, and it has been mentioned from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

﴿وَشَاهِدٍ وَمَشْهُودٍ﴾ The words *shahid* (witness) and *mashhud* (witnessed) may be taken as from *al-shahada* (testimony) concerning a matter, or from the meaning of *al-huduur* (presence). The object is omitted, and its implied form is: witnessed against, or witnessed to, or witnessed in.

People have differed greatly in the interpretation of *al-shahid* and *al-mashhud*. Their statements on *al-shahid* can be summarized as sixteen opinions, and against them on *al-mashhud* there are thirty-two opinions.

The first: *al-shahid* is Allah, Exalted, because of His saying ﴿وَكَفَىٰ بِٱللَّهِ شَهِيداً﴾ [An-Nisa: 79, 166; Al-Fath: 28]. On this view, *al-mashhud* may have three meanings: the first is that it is creation, in the sense that He witnesses over them; the second is that it is deeds, in the sense that He witnesses them; the third is the Day of Resurrection, in the sense that He is present in it, i.e., attends for reckoning and recompense, or that testimony is given over people in it.

The second opinion: *al-shahid* is Muhammad ﷺ, because of His saying: ﴿لِيَكُونَ ٱلرَّسُولُ شَهِيداً عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [Al-Hajj: 78]. On this view, *al-mashhud* may be his community, because he witnesses over them, or their deeds, because he witnesses them, or the Day of Resurrection, because he is present in it, i.e., attends, or testimony is given over the community in it.

The third: *al-shahid* is the community of Muhammad ﷺ, because of His saying: ﴿لِّتَكُونُواْ شُهَدَآءَ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 143]. On this view, *al-mashhud* is all the other nations, because they (the community) witness over them, because of His saying: ﴿وَكُنتُ عَلَيْهِمْ شَهِيداً مَّا دُمْتُ فِيهِمْ﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 117], or their deeds, or the Day of Resurrection.

The fifth: *al-shahid* is all the prophets, and *al-mashhud* is their communities, because every prophet witnesses over his community; or the testimony is to their deeds; or the Day of Resurrection, because it is present in it.

The sixth: *al-shahid* is the guardian angels, and *al-mashhud* is people, because the angels witness over them; or the deeds, because the angels witness them; or the Day of Resurrection; or the Dawn Prayer, because of His saying: ﴿إِنَّ قُرْآنَ ٱلْفَجْرِ كَانَ مَشْهُوداً﴾ [Al-Isra: 78].

The seventh: *al-shahid* is all people, because they are present on the Day of Resurrection, i.e., they attend it, and *al-mashhud* is the Day of Resurrection, because of His saying: ﴿وَذَلِكَ يَوْمٌ مَّشْهُودٌ﴾ [Hud: 103].

The eighth: *al-shahid* is the limbs, and *al-mashhud 'alayhi* (the one testified against) is their owners, because of His saying: ﴿يَوْمَ تَشْهَدُ عَلَيْهِمْ أَلْسِنَتُهُمْ وَأَيْدِيهِمْ وَأَرْجُلُهُمْ﴾ [An-Nur: 24]; or the deeds, because the limbs testify to them on the Day of Resurrection, since testimony takes place in it.

The ninth: *al-shahid* is Allah, the angels and those of knowledge, because of His saying: ﴿شَهِدَ ٱللَّهُ أَنَّهُ لاَ إِلَـٰهَ إِلاَّ هُوَ وَٱلْمَلاَئِكَةُ وَأُوْلُواْ ٱلْعِلْمِ﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 18], and *al-mashhud bihi* (that which is testified to) is the Oneness (of Allah).

The tenth: *al-shahid* is all created beings, and *al-mashhud bihi* is the existence of their Creator and the affirmation of His attributes, such as life, power and others.

The eleventh: *al-shahid* is the star, because of what has come in the hadith: "There is no prayer after the 'Asr until the *shahid* rises," and the *shahid* is the star. On this view, *al-mashhud* is the night and the day, because the star testifies to the end of the day and the entry of the night.

The twelfth: *al-shahid* is the Black Stone, and *al-mashhud* is the people who perform Hajj.

The thirteenth: it is related from the Prophet ﷺ that *al-shahid* is Friday and *al-mashhud* is the Day of 'Arafah, because Friday testifies to the deeds, and the Day of 'Arafah is attended by a great multitude of people.

The fourteenth: *al-shahid* is the Day of 'Arafah and *al-mashhud* is the Day of Sacrifice (al-Nahr), as said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

The fifteenth: *al-shahid* is the Day of Tarwiyah and *al-mashhud* is the Day of 'Arafah.

The sixteenth: *al-shahid* is Monday and *al-mashhud* is Friday.

﴿قُتِلَ أَصْحَابُ ٱلأُخْدُودِ﴾ The discussion here falls into three sections.

The first: concerning the answer to the oath, and there are four opinions on it. The first is that it is His saying: ﴿إِنَّ بَطْشَ رَبِّكَ لَشَدِيدٌ﴾ [Al-Buruj: 12]. The second is that it is: ﴿إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ فَتَنُواْ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَٱلْمُؤْمِنَاتِ﴾ [Al-Buruj: 10]. These two opinions are weak, because of the distance between the oath and the answer. The third is that it is "Qutila Ashab al-Ukhdud" (the companions of the trench were killed), with the implied meaning: "Surely they were killed." The fourth is that it is omitted, and is indicated by "Qutila Ashab al-Ukhdud," with the implied meaning: "Surely these disbelievers have been killed as the companions of the trench were killed." This is because the disbelievers of Quraysh used to torture those among their people who had embraced Islam, to make them turn back from Islam. So Allah mentioned the story of the companions of the trench as a warning to the disbelievers and as a consolation to the tortured Muslims.

The second section: explanation of its wording. As for *qutila*, it has been disputed whether it is a supplication or a statement; and whether it means killing literally or cursing. As for *al-ukhdud*, it is a cleft in the earth like a trench or the like. As for *ashab al-ukhdud*, it may mean the disbelievers who used to burn the believers in the trench, or it may mean the believers in the trench, or the believers who were burned in it. Then the killing would be a literal statement. The first is more apparent.

The third section: the story of the companions of the trench, which has four opinions. The first is what has come from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a long hadith, whose meaning is: a disbelieving king made the people of his city embrace (a false religion), so he ordered a trench to be dug, and it was dug at the mouths of the roads, and fires were kindled in it. He said: "Whoever does not turn back from his religion, throw him into it." They did so, until a woman came with a child of hers, and she hesitated to throw herself into it. The boy said to her: "O mother, be patient, for you are upon the truth."

The second: a king committed incest with his sister, then wanted to make marriage with sisters lawful for the people. Some people obeyed him, and among them the Magians took that (practice). Some people disobeyed him, so he dug a trench for them and burned them in it with fire.

The third opinion: the prophet of the companions of the trench was an Abyssinian, and the Abyssinians are the remnant of the companions of the trench.

The fourth opinion: the companions of the trench were Dhu Nuwas, who is mentioned in the story of 'Abdullah ibn al-Tamir which is widely known. It is possible that Dhu Nuwas is the king whom the Prophet ﷺ mentioned, so this opinion agrees with the first, for Dhu Nuwas dug a trench, kindled fires in it, and threw into it everyone who affirmed the Oneness of Allah Exalted and followed the righteous servant 'Abdullah ibn al-Tamir.

ٱلنَّارِ ذَاتِ ٱلْوَقُودِ — "the Fire, fueled with wood" (al-nār) is a substitute (badal) for al-ukhdūd (the trench), a badal ishtimāl (substitute of inclusion). Al-wuqūd is that with which the fire is kindled (fuel). The purpose of the description is to characterize the fire as intense and great.

إِذْ هُمْ عَلَيْهَا قُعُودٌ — The pronoun refers to the disbelievers who used to burn the believers in the trench, and they are the People of the Trench according to the most apparent view. The governing element (al-āmil) in "idh" is the word "qutila" (were cursed/killed). It is narrated that the fire burned twenty thousand of the believers, and it was said seventy thousand. So "qutila" in this case carries the sense of "luʿina" (were cursed), meaning they were cursed when they sat by the fire to burn the believers. It is also narrated that God sent a wind upon the believers which seized their souls, and the fire came out and burned the disbelievers who were beside it; so "qutila" in this case carries its literal meaning of killing, i.e., the fire killed them. It was also said that the pronoun in "idh hum" refers to the believers. The first view is more well-known and more apparent, because of His saying:

وَهُمْ عَلَىٰ مَا يَفْعَلُونَ بِٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ شُهُودٌ — "and they were witnesses to what they did to the believers." This may carry the sense of testimony, i.e., some of them bear witness for others before the king that he carried out what the king ordered, namely the burning; or they bear witness against themselves on the Day of Resurrection; or it may carry the sense of presence, i.e., they were present at that act.

وَمَا نَقَمُواْ مِنْهُمْ إِلاَّ أَن يُؤْمِنُواْ بِٱللَّهِ — "They did not resent them except that they believed in God," meaning the disbelievers did not object to the believers except that they believed in God, and this is not something that should be objected to. If it is asked: why did He say "an yu'minū" (that they believe) in the present tense and not "āmanū" (they believed) in the past tense, since the event had already occurred? The answer: the punishment was only for their persistence in faith; had they disbelieved in the future, they would not have tortured them. Therefore He mentioned it in the future tense, as if He said: "except that they persist in faith."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 85, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women﴾ If this verse refers to the People of the Trench (Ashab al-Ukhdud), then "fitnah" here means burning. If it refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, then "fitnah" means trial and torment. The latter is more evident, due to His saying: ﴿then they did not repent﴾, for the People of the Trench did not repent but died upon their disbelief. As for Quraysh, some of them embraced Islam and repented. The verse is evidence that when a disbeliever embraces Islam, what he did in the state of his disbelief is forgiven, due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Islam erases what came before it."

﴿And for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾ It may be in the Hereafter, in which case it is an emphasis of the punishment of Hell, or a kind of punishment in addition to the punishment of Hell. It may also mean in this world, according to the narration that the disbelievers, the People of the Trench, were burned by the fire.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 85, verse 12–15:

﴿Indeed, the seizing of your Lord is severe.﴾ Al-batsh (seizing) means taking with strength and swiftness. ﴿Indeed, it is He who originates and repeats.﴾ That is, He originates creation with the first creation, and repeats them with the final creation for resurrection. It is also said: He originates the seizing and repeats it, meaning He seizes them in this world and the Hereafter. The first (interpretation) is more apparent and more preferable because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, He originates creation, then repeats it﴾ [Yunus: 4]. We have mentioned al-Wadud (the Most Loving) in the lexicographical discussion. ﴿Owner of the Throne, the Glorious﴾ He attributed the Throne to Allah and singled it out for mention because the Throne is the greatest of the created things. Al-majid (the Glorious) derives from al-majd, which is nobility and elevation of rank. Al-Majid has been read in the nominative (majīdun) as an adjective of "Owner of the Throne," and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive (majīdi) as an adjective of "the Throne."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 85, verse 17:

﴿Has there come to you﴾ is a form of interrogation (tawqif) intended to draw attention and to emphasize the gravity of the matter. The mention of the armies is intended to threaten the disbelievers and to comfort the Prophet (ﷺ).
And Allah encompasses them from behind them. This is a threat to them: its meaning is that they cannot escape Him; rather His punishment will reach them whenever He wills.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 85, verse 22:

﴿In a Preserved Tablet﴾ means the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) that is in the heavens. It is also recited as "mahfuzin" in the genitive, as an attribute of "lawh" (tablet). Nafi' recited "mahfuzun" in the nominative, as an attribute of "al-Qur'an," meaning: God preserved it from alteration and change, or the believers preserved it in their hearts.
